stances.claim: False material representation is the exclusive ground for cancelling a COC -- 'no other possible ground,' as the Second Division correctly ruled.
BBM's COC representations were 'material' (he averred all qualifications and no ineligibilities) -- the Second Division was right on the first element.
The Second Division was wrong to conclude that BBM was 'no longer a public officer' on March 18, 1986 -- Panganiban disagrees with this factual-legal claim.
stances.rhetorical_move: express dissent on the constitutional-continuity question

stances.claim: The Second Division's third-element holding (no deliberate attempt to mislead because the CA Decision did not categorically apprise BBM) is 'debatable.'

Adding moral turpitude and mandatory-imprisonment-over-18-months grounds to a Section 78 cancellation petition is a procedural violation that could have justified outright dismissal -- but the Second Division generously addressed the merits.

The Resolution correctly observed that the petitioners 'deliberately misquoted' the law by characterizing imprisonment as mandatory -- the original law gave the courts discretion to impose fine OR imprisonment OR both; mandatory imprisonment came only with the Jan. 1, 1988 amendment.
stances.rhetorical_move: textual rebuke of petitioners on statutory accuracy

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban walks lay readers through the Comelec Second Division's 32-page, unanimous Resolution (Presiding Commissioner Socorro B. Inting, with Antonio T. Kho Jr. concurring via Separate Opinion, and Rey E. Bulay) dismissing the petition to cancel Bongbong Marcos's Certificate of Candidacy. He agrees with the Resolution that false material representation is the exclusive ground for COC cancellation under Section 78 of the OEC, and that adding moral-turpitude and mandatory-imprisonment-over-18-months grounds confuses cancellation with disqualification under Section 12. He concurs that BBM's COC statements were 'material' but parts ways with the Division's rejection of falsity: he disagrees that BBM 'ceased to be a public officer' on March 18, 1986 (the ITR filing deadline for tax year 1985) and flags as 'debatable' the third-element holding that BBM lacked deliberate intent to mislead since the CA Decision did not categorically apprise him of perpetual ineligibility. He records the Resolution's reliance on Republic v. Marcos (Aug. 4, 2009) for the proposition that failure to file ITR is not a crime of moral turpitude, and its observation that the petitioners 'deliberately misquoted' the original tax law, which gave courts discretion between fine, imprisonment, or both -- mandatory imprisonment only entered with the Jan. 1, 1988 amendment. Out of deference to Theodore O. Te's anticipated motion for reconsideration the next day, Panganiban refrains from full commentary -- modeling the kind of measured doctrinal summary he says lay readers need.
